content:
A line of argument found in several writings by people who left Islam runs as follows. The Prophet ﷺ was an orphan, handed from one carer to another and robbed of love, which left him with deep insecurity. He grew into a narcissist, hungry for power and attention. He then used religion as the tool, and made God his own alter ego. The writers add a list of tyrants of the twentieth century, to show the type.

This is an argument about a man's mind, drawn from a distance of fourteen centuries. These six entries check the facts the argument relies on, set the conduct recorded in the sources beside the label, and ask whether the method can bear the weight put on it. The article judges no living person, and it concedes that the sources record hard things about the Prophet ﷺ that readers are free to examine. The related articles are the claim that Muhammad was a false prophet, who wrote the Quran and whether Muslims worship Muhammad.

The claim has four steps. First, the early losses: a father dead before his birth, a mother who gave him to a wet nurse, and an upbringing among many carers. Second, a psychological conclusion drawn from them, that a child without secure love grows into an adult who craves recognition. Third, the label of narcissism, with a list of dictators as comparison. Fourth, the theory that a religion served him as an instrument and that the God he spoke for was a projection of himself.

Each step depends on the one before. If the first step is wrong in its facts, the second has nothing to stand on. If the second is a guess, the third is a verdict on a guess. The fourth cannot be tested at all. A fair assessment goes through them in order, and the first step is the one that can be checked against the sources.

Verdict: the claim is a chain, and every link is a different kind of statement. Only the first is a matter of record.

The Quran says: "Did He not find you an orphan and give [you] refuge? And He found you lost and guided [you], and He found you poor and made [you] self-sufficient" (93:6-8).[1] The orphanhood is stated in the scripture itself, and nobody who reads the Prophet's biography denies it.

The biographies in the tradition of Ibn Isḥāq say that his father ʿAbdullāh died before he was born, that he was given to a wet nurse of the Banū Saʿd named Ḥalīma, and that his mother Āmina died at al-Abwāʾ, on the road between Mecca and Medina, when he was six. His grandfather ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib cared for him until he died, when the boy was about eight, and his uncle Abū Ṭālib then took him in.[2] The accounts differ on how long Ḥalīma nursed him.

Two claims in the argument are not in these accounts. The accounts read for this article do not give five carers before the age of eight. They name a wet nurse, a mother, a grandfather and an uncle. They also do not say that his mother gave him up so that she could find another husband. They say she took him to visit relatives and died on the road. The first part, the nursing by a woman of a desert tribe, was a custom among the families of Mecca. This is stated from general knowledge and the accounts above, and it was not checked in a critical edition. Verdict: the early loss is real. The details added to it are not in the sources.

Narcissism, as the term is used in the argument, means a hunger for admiration and a need to be above others. The sources report the Prophet ﷺ differently. When ʿĀʾisha was asked what he did in his house, she said, "He used to keep himself busy serving his family and when it was the time for prayer he would go for it."[3] She also said that whenever he was given a choice between two matters he took the easier unless it was sinful, and that he never took revenge for himself, only when God's limits were broken.[4]

When he died he left no money, no slave and nothing else but his white mule, his arms and a piece of land he had given in charity.[5] A man who sought power for its rewards left a smaller estate than a tradesman.

The clearest instance is an eclipse. The sun eclipsed on the day his son Ibrāhīm died, and people said that it was for his death. He answered, "The sun and the moon do not eclipse because of the death or life of someone. When you see the eclipse pray and invoke Allah."[6] A man hungry for signs of his own greatness would have taken the credit. He stopped it. Verdict: the recorded conduct runs against the label. Narcissism may fit a man who needs attention, and it does not fit a man who turns attention away.

The book that the argument calls the work of his ego contains public corrections of him. In 80:1-10, God says that the Prophet ﷺ "frowned and turned away" because a blind man interrupted him while he was speaking to the nobles of Mecca, and tells him that he gave attention to the one who thought himself without need and was distracted from the one who came striving.[7]

Verse 66:1 asks, "why do you prohibit [yourself from] what Allah has made lawful for you, seeking the approval of your wives?" Verse 9:43 says: "Allah has pardoned you, [O Muhammad, but] why did you give them permission [to remain behind]?" Verse 8:67 says that it is "not for a prophet to have captives [of war] until he inflicts a massacre", which criticises a decision taken after Badr.[8]

Verse 33:37 says that he concealed within himself what God was to disclose, and "feared the people, while Allah has more right that you fear Him". Verse 3:128 tells him that the decision is not his.[9] These verses are recited in public and preserved as part of the text for fourteen centuries. If the Prophet ﷺ were an author who wrote God as a mirror of himself, he chose a strange mirror. Verdict: a text that rebukes its messenger in public is not the product of vanity. The best that can be said for the alternative is that it is an odd form of vanity.

The Quran tells him to say: "I am only a man like you, to whom has been revealed that your god is one God" (18:110).[10] It tells him to say: "I hold not for myself [the power of] benefit or harm, except what Allah has willed. And if I knew the unseen, I could have acquired much wealth" (7:188), and "I do not tell you that I have the depositories [containing the provision] of Allah or that I know the unseen, nor do I tell you that I am an angel" (6:50).[11]

It says to him, "you are only a reminder. You are not over them a controller" (88:21-22), and "would you compel the people in order that they become believers?" (10:99).[12] Verse 3:79 says that it is not for any prophet to tell the people, "Be servants to me rather than Allah".[13]

A man seeking worship for himself would not be given these lines. Al-Fārūqī's first principle, the line between Creator and creature, is the one the Prophet ﷺ is made to repeat here: he is on the creature's side of it, and he says so.[14] The idea that God in the Quran is his "alter ego" ignores that the Quran sets limits on the messenger in the messenger's own voice. Verdict: he is made to disclaim exactly what the label says he wanted.

Psychiatry diagnoses living people by examining them. A diagnosis at a distance of fourteen centuries uses sources written by followers, sources written by opponents, and a modern checklist applied to a seventh-century Arab merchant. Professional bodies tell their members not to diagnose public figures they have not examined. This is stated from general knowledge, and no code of ethics was checked on a page for this article.

The method also proves too much. The same childhood that is said to make a narcissist could be said to make an empathic man, one who knew what it was to be an orphan and therefore commanded kindness to orphans (93:9). Anyone can build a story from any facts, and a story that fits every outcome tells nothing. The list of twentieth-century tyrants set beside him is a guilt-by-category argument, and it needs actual comparison on the facts, such as the scale of deaths. The article on the raids and the conquest of Mecca sets out what the sources record.

A fair critic may still examine the Prophet's conduct, and the sources show actions that readers judge hard, among them the judgement on Banū Qurayẓa and wars of expulsion. Muslim sources report that he said, "I will expel the Jews and Christians from the Arabian Peninsula", and also that he let the Jews of Khaybar remain on the land until ʿUmar removed them.[15] These deserve scrutiny on their own terms, and the article on the Jewish tribes gives them that. They are matters of conduct to be argued from the sources. A diagnosis does not add to them. Verdict: the diagnosis adds nothing the sources do not already give, and it replaces evidence with a label.

The bottom line

The Prophet ﷺ was an orphan, and the Quran says so. The details added to that fact in the argument, the many carers and the mother who left for a new husband, are not in the accounts read here. The conduct recorded of him is of a man who served his household, left nothing, refused credit for an eclipse and was corrected in public by the book he brought. His own lines in that book disclaim power, the unseen and any claim to be served.

A critic of his conduct has the sources to work with, and they are open. A critic who prefers a diagnosis has chosen a method that cannot be tested, applied to a man who cannot be examined. Allāhu aʿlam.

Notes

  1. Quran 93:6-9, Saheeh International translation, read on the Quran.com API.
  2. Ibn Isḥāq's biography as summarised on the Muhammad: Legacy of a Prophet timeline at PBS (pbs.org/muhammad) and in a reproduction of the Ibn Isḥāq text on a Santa Rosa Junior College course page, read through a web search for this article. These are traditional accounts and secondary summaries; they were not checked in a critical edition, and the sources differ on how long Ḥalīma nursed him.
  3. Sahih al-Bukhari 676, report of al-Aswad on what the Prophet did in his house, read in the English text of the hadith-api edition, where it stands as book 10, hadith 70; the printed page was not checked.
  4. Sahih al-Bukhari 3560, report of ʿĀʾisha, same edition (book 61, hadith 69).
  5. Sahih al-Bukhari 2739, report of ʿAmr ibn al-Ḥārith, same edition (book 55, hadith 2).
  6. Sahih al-Bukhari 1043, report of al-Mughīra ibn Shuʿba, same edition (book 16, hadith 4).
  7. Quran 80:1-10, Saheeh International. That the blind man was ʿAbdullāh ibn Umm Maktūm and the Prophet was speaking with Meccan nobles is the common account and is not cited to a source here.
  8. Quran 66:1, 9:43 and 8:67, Saheeh International. That 8:67 refers to the decision on the prisoners after Badr is the common reading and was not checked on a page.
  9. Quran 33:37 and 3:128, Saheeh International.
  10. Quran 18:110, Saheeh International.
  11. Quran 7:188 and 6:50, Saheeh International.
  12. Quran 88:21-22 and 10:99, Saheeh International.
  13. Quran 3:79, Saheeh International.
  14. Al-Fārūqī, Al Tawhid: Its Implications for Thought and Life (International Institute of Islamic Thought, 2nd edition, 1992), chapter 1, on the duality of Creator and creature, as set out in the project's Faruqian core document; the page was not rechecked for this article.
  15. Sahih Muslim, report of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, "I will expel the Jews and Christians from the Arabian Peninsula", read in English as book 32, hadith 75 in the hadith-api edition; and the report of Ibn ʿUmar on the Jews of Khaybar remaining until ʿUmar removed them to Taymāʾ and Arīḥā, read as book 22, hadith 6.
